title: Shepard Tone Synthesizer — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Shepard Tone Synthesizer's rich face, its first round, a Study offered as a proposal: two walks made for the stages that had no test a reader could play (the still drone, and the free seam done blind), and beside every other stage the renders and instruments its steward already made, laid in the order that walks up to each one's test. I grow when the instrument grows a stage; I never hold the entry's words.

pieces.title: how the Shepard tone works · the May chart
pieces.caption: Ten voices (the chart says partials) rising in lockstep through one fixed Gaussian window, drawn in log frequency. Each line enters at the bottom, near silent, and leaves at the top, near silent. Its window sits near 300 Hz on A, not on C4 as the example below has it.
pieces.near: The Shepard tone is a psychoacoustic illusion

pieces.title: the endless ascent · May render, second take
pieces.caption: Twelve seconds of climb, the mechanism above as sound. This is the second take: in the first, Loudon heard clicks, and the fix was to wrap each voice on its own, at the moment its level is near zero. Keep ascending; arrive nowhere.

verdicts.why: Illustrates rather than tests, but the caption says honestly where it disagrees with the text (window near 300 Hz on A, not C4), which sets up offer 2. Note: 'near silent' at entry is about −16 dB on the chart's own curve.
The mechanism as sound; the caption's history (clicks from every octave snapping back, fixed by a per-voice wrap near zero) matches the 2026-05-04 Proof Showcase v2.

pieces.title: the April session page · Stage 1, Ableton
pieces.caption: **The rack, built.** The April Loud’n Live session for this design: nine Pitch devices in a MIDI Effect Rack, one AutoFilter on the sum as the Shepard window, and a picture of the stack cycling through it. Gathered as it was. One step has aged: it offers a saw as well as a sine, and Stage 4 measured that a filter on the sum lets a saw’s wrapping voice in as a thump (the correction under Global Shepard Filter). Keep the voices sines for this rack.

verdicts.why: A real thing to make rather than a test; the caption flags its one aged step (line 530 offers a saw) against Stage 4's measurement.

pieces.title: every octave gliding on its own · September
pieces.caption: **The challenge, heard.** The stack with each voice gliding separately: the octaves arrive at different times and the one note smears apart.

pieces.title: one glide for the whole stack · 450 ms · September
pieces.caption: **The solution, heard.** The same glide time, one glide for every octave: a single voice sliding, the way the paragraph above describes.

pieces.file: Shepard Tone Synthesizer — rich — the still drone.html
pieces.caption: **Stage 1, walked up to its test.** One sine at C4; its octaves added one at a time; the window, in log2(Hz) and in Hz; then the test: pull one voice off its octave, or stretch them all, and hear when seven sines stop being one note. The page says the still stack fuses. It doesn’t say how far a voice can stray before it is two, so that number is yours. The engine is shepard_synth.py’s: C1 to C7, σ 1 octave on C4.
pieces.near: This is the claim the static drone makes

pieces.title: the endless ascent · May render, first take
pieces.caption: **A seam that was not free.** The first May render, where every voice snapped back at once at the loop point. Loudon heard clicks: “I am hearing clicks at a few moments.” The second take, in How Shepard Tones Work, wraps each voice alone while it is quiet, and the clicks went.
pieces.near: The lesson Stage 2 teaches that the still drone could not

pieces.file: Shepard Tone Synthesizer — rich — the free seam.html
pieces.caption: **Stage 2, tested blind.** The still drone, one semitone step, twelve steps that come home, the seam lit red with its level as it leaves and lands. Then the test: twelve steps with the picture and the readout covered, and you press when you hear the join. Two switches take away, one at a time, the two things this section says hide the seam: open the window wide, or let the wrap land a semitone off. If the page is right, the page’s window with an on-octave wrap scores near chance. Measured, not heard: in the page’s window the wrapping voice leaves 35 dB and lands 33 dB under the loudest voice.

pieces.title: the glide, playable · October
pieces.caption: **The test: drift on an endless climb.** Press *start sound*, then *endless up*, and raise *drift between octaves*: the spoke fans out and the readout gives the split in cents. The section predicts about 16 ¢ at 2 semitones a second with ±30 % drift, held for as long as the climb lasts. Switch the glide to *Hz slew, per voice* for the patching mistake.

verdicts.file: Shepard Tone Synthesizer — rich — the still drone.html
verdicts.why: Step 3 stands a Gaussian drawn on a linear Hz axis in for the page's 'literal bandpass', so it confirms the sentence by construction; a real 2-pole bandpass at C4 is symmetric in octaves (C3 = C5 = −3.0 dB, 28.7 % below and above). Add that bandpass as a fourth window with the low/high energy readout, rename the Hz bell for what it is, and let step 3 ask rather than answer; engine, walk and step 4 stand.
The counter-case beside 'the seam is free': a wrap that clicked because every voice snapped at once; the quote is sourced in the May showcase.

verdicts.file: Shepard Tone Synthesizer — rich — the free seam.html
verdicts.why: A real blind test with right chance figures and one wrap per trial, but it calls session-2's window (600 Hz, σ 1.6) 'the page's', and in that window the semitone-off wrap lands 33.2 dB down and peaks at −19.8 dB, so page/wrong will likely score near chance and read as 'octave equivalence does nothing'. Relabel the window, name the two comparisons (page/octave vs wide/octave; wide/octave vs wide/wrong), say page/wrong is expected near chance, and ask for headphones (27 Hz and 14 kHz ends); tally and engine stand.

offers.what: Stage 2: the free-seam piece measured where the forgiving happens. In the page's window (600 Hz, σ 1.6 oct) the wrapping voice leaves 34.8 dB and lands 33.2 dB under the loudest voice, and the summed level moves 0.0003 dB across the wrap, so the window alone keeps the join quiet; octave equivalence decides what the landed voice becomes as it climbs (a wrong-landing wrap stays under −19.8 dB for the rest of a 12-step climb). 'In a world without octave equivalence that drop would be a catastrophe' may want to say that the window has already put the voice ~35 dB down at both ends. Not heard; the blind trial is for Loudon's ear.

The worked example centres the window on C4 but puts C2 and C3 in the sweet spot and has C5 and C6 fading. Under any window symmetric in octaves on C4, C3 and C5 match (−4.3 dB at σ 1 oct) and C2 and C6 match (−17.4 dB). Suggest: C3, C4 and C5 in the sweet spot; C2 and C6 fading; C1 and C7 almost gone. Measured on the still-drone piece's engine.

'A 2-octave window is typical (about 1.4 × center frequency)': a band from fc/2 to 2fc is 1.5 × fc wide, Q = 2/3 ≈ 0.67. Arithmetic, not a piece. 'All 128 MIDI octaves' (here and in Design Challenge 5) reads as 128 MIDI notes, about ten and a half octaves.

Stage 1 says 'Pair with Stage 1 above', and Stages 2 to 4 say the same, but the page has no Stage headings above Theory; the stages live in the scroll's plan and the bundle. Suggest 'Pair with the Stage 1 build (…)' or drop 'above'.
